newsitem.title: UK: British soldier dies after IRA bombing.
newsitem.headline: British soldier dies after IRA bombing.

text.p: A soldier injured in an IRA bombing attack on Britain's military headquarters in Northern Ireland died on Friday, security forces said.

Warrant Officer Class One James Bradwell was the first British soldier to be killed by the Irish Republican Army since it called a 17-month ceasefire in September 1994. The ceasefire ended in February.
"We can confirm that he has died from injuries received in the bombing," a British army spokesman told Reuters.
Irish Republican Army guerrillas breached high security at the Lisburn garrison, 10 miles (15km) south of Belfast, on Monday and detonated two 500lb (225kg) carbombs without warning.
Bradwell, 43, of the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, who was married with three children, received 60 percent burns when the bombs exploded 20 minutes apart.
Nine other soldiers and 21 civilians were injured.
The attack marked a switch in tactics by the IRA who had confined their campaign since February to bombs in British mainland cities, and one at a British military base in Germany.
The bombing dealt a shattering blow to Northern Irish peace efforts and stoked fears of a backlash by pro-British Protestant guerrillas who called a ceasefire in October 1994.
Protestant extremists fighting to safeguard British rule are expected to announce shortly whether they will stick to their truce.
Bradwell was the first soldier killed in a guerrilla attack while on duty in the British province since May 1994.
IRA guerrillas shot dead two off-duty Protestant members of the locally-recruited Royal Irish Regiment, a regiment of the British Army, in May and August that year.

The IRA called its original ceasefire in an abortive move to get its Sinn Fein political arm into peace talks. It ditched the truce saying it was frustrated over Britain's demand that the guerrillas disarm before Sinn Fein was allowed to join negotiations.

Britain and Ireland, pursuing a joint political strategy to end generations of division between the region's majority pro-British Protestants and minority Catholics, say Sinn Fein will not be admitted to current multi-party talks until the IRA calls off its campaign.
